parts.note: Lab is the short form of the UK Labour Party
oratory is the art of public speaking, i.e. rhetoric

explanation.surface: A political party's training ground for speechmaking.
explanation.definitionFit: A laboratory is a place where scientific work and experiments are carried out, a kind of workshop.

explanation.surface: A question about whether something final will hold.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective it means final or ultimate; as a verb it means to endure or stay usable, as food does when it keeps.

clue.text: Purchased around Russia and delivered here

indicators.note: around tells us the word for purchased is wrapped about the Russia letter

parts.note: purchased means bought
R is the international vehicle code for Russia

explanation.surface: Goods bought in Russia and shipped over to us.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring something is to carry or deliver it towards the speaker's place.

indicators.note: a form of the words means their letters reshaped into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A German translation of the verb to totter, abandoned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'totter' looks like the verb to wobble, but it is old British slang for a scrap collector who went round streets buying rags and junk from a horse and cart.
explanation.definitionFit: Totter is British slang for a street dealer in old clothes and scrap, collected door to door.

indicators.note: in a down clue over means the first piece sits above the second

parts.note: a cross looks like X, the Roman numeral for ten
the Ure is a river in Yorkshire, a crossword favourite

explanation.surface: Instructions to cross a river while keeping one's job.
explanation.definitionFit: Tenure is the period or fact of occupying a post, the holding of a position.

parts.note: read not as a door mechanism but as locks of hair shaped like coiled springs

explanation.definitionFit: These are curled tresses of hair that spiral like little springs.

parts.note: L is the standard abbreviation for large, as on clothing labels
an oaf is a clumsy, boorish lout

explanation.surface: A lazy, hulking lout.
explanation.definitionFit: To loaf is to laze about doing nothing, so it is a verb meaning to idle.

parts.note: or is the heraldic word for gold
providing means on condition that, i.e. if
ice is slang for diamonds

explanation.surface: The unveiling of a gold piece set with diamonds.
explanation.definitionFit: An orifice is a hole or aperture, an opening into something.

clue.text: In which the off is off?

definitions.text: In which the off is off?

parts.words: In which the off is off?
parts.note: the off is the start of a race; here that start is cancelled and has to be rerun

explanation.definitionFit: In racing, a premature start by a competitor means the race must be restarted, so the beginning is void.

clue.text: Japanese military dictator tense at heart in such a wedding…

indicators.note: at heart puts the tense letter into the centre of the dictator's title

parts.note: a shogun was a hereditary military ruler of Japan
T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: A Japanese warlord grows nervous during a hurried marriage ceremony.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links this clue to the next, where the marriage theme continues.
explanation.definitionFit: A forced marriage, supposedly arranged under threat from the bride's father, is known by this firearm name.

clue.text: … well-versed in Latin order of the marriage

indicators.note: in places the knowledgeable word inside the rearranged letters
putting the word Latin in a new order means its letters are rearranged

parts.note: to be up on a subject is to be well-versed in it

explanation.surface: An expert in the Latin order of service for a wedding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'well-versed' looks like a description of a poet, but it means being up on something; 'order' is the rearranging signal, not a church service.
explanation.definitionFit: Nuptial is an adjective meaning relating to a wedding or matrimony.

parts.note: patent means obvious or plainly visible
kid is soft leather made from young goatskin, so it is an example of leather

explanation.surface: Asks what kind of shoes would make a child stand out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'kid' suggests a child, but it is the goatskin material; the question mark marks it as one example of the material.
explanation.definitionFit: Glossy varnished hide is the material of shiny formal shoes, so the phrase names that kind of footwear.

clue.text: Officer's three-wheeler has everybody out in it

parts.note: a general is a senior army officer; the possessive supplies the extra S
a trike is a tricycle, a three-wheeled vehicle

explanation.surface: A senior officer's tricycle carries all his men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'everybody out' is the union cry for all workers to down tools, so the definition describes a nationwide stoppage.
explanation.definitionFit: A stoppage by workers across all industries at once means every worker walks out.

clue.text: Base nature of soldier up to join high society

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the soldier word is read from the bottom

parts.note: GI is an American soldier
the nobility are the aristocratic upper class

explanation.surface: A soldier climbing the ranks to join the aristocracy.
explanation.definitionFit: Being base means lowly and dishonourable, the opposite of noble character.

explanation.surface: A bird described as huge in size.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jay' looks like the bird but is the first name of the hero of Fitzgerald's novel The Great Gatsby; 'great in volume' means named after Great in a book.
explanation.definitionFit: Jay is the forename of Fitzgerald's hero, and the novel's title puts Great before his surname.

clue.text: Being extremely broke is the hardest condition

explanation.surface: Having no money at all is the toughest situation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stony broke' is British slang for having no money at all, so the superlative means most penniless.
explanation.definitionFit: Stony means penniless in slang and also rock-like, so the superlative covers most skint and most rigid.

clue.text: Barney, university male, dressed in silver

indicators.note: dressed in means the university and male letters are clothed by the silver word

parts.note: argent is the heraldic word for silver

explanation.surface: Someone called Barney, a male student, wearing silver.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barney' looks like a man's name, but it is British slang for a noisy quarrel.
explanation.definitionFit: Barney is British slang for a row or noisy quarrel.

explanation.surface: A plain, unremarkable coat-of-arms design.
explanation.definitionFit: It means commonplace and unremarkable; in heraldry it is also a simple bold charge such as a cross or chevron.

clue.text: Figure of endless torture after last month

indicators.note: after puts the torture word behind the month abbreviation

parts.note: Dec is short for December, the last month of the year

indicators.note: endless means the final letter of the torture word is dropped

parts.note: agony is extreme suffering, torture

explanation.surface: A shape produced by unending torment following December.
explanation.definitionFit: A decagon is a ten-sided plane shape, a geometric figure.

parts.note: to lower means to reduce or bring down

explanation.surface: A woman cutting back on dairy cream.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cream' suggests the dairy product, but it means the best part, as in the flower of youth.
explanation.definitionFit: Flower can mean the finest or choicest part, just as cream does in the cream of society.

clue.text: Court bringing up orange-seller? That's like some yam!

parts.note: to court someone is to woo them

indicators.note: in a down clue bringing up means the seller's name is read upwards

parts.note: Nell Gwyn sold oranges in a London theatre before becoming the mistress of Charles II

explanation.surface: Wooing an orange-seller makes for a tall story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bringing up' turns NELL into LLEN. The scanned 'yam' is a misreading of 'yarn', which suggests a tale but here is thread spun from fleece.
explanation.definitionFit: Woollen describes thread or cloth spun from sheep's fleece, as some knitting yarn is.

clue.text: Cut off and depressed, having lost one shilling

indicators.note: having means the depressed word holds the one and shilling letters inside it

parts.note: to feel down is to be depressed
I is the Roman numeral for one
s was the abbreviation for the old British shilling

explanation.surface: Disinherited and miserable after being left just one shilling.
explanation.walkthrough: Being 'cut off with a shilling' was the traditional way to disinherit an heir in a will; the shilling was an old British coin.
explanation.definitionFit: To disown a child is to renounce them, as when cutting them off from an inheritance.

clue.text: No duo can mimic result of being so cut off

indicators.note: the result of the phrase means what its letters produce when rearranged

explanation.surface: Two performers cannot imitate what isolation produces.
explanation.definitionFit: Incommunicado means unable or not allowed to contact anyone, isolated from communication.

explanation.surface: Spinning bowlers who are first-rate.
explanation.definitionFit: Spinning toys are called this, and as slang the same word means the very best.

indicators.note: to sort the word genuine is to rearrange its letters

explanation.surface: A naive young woman who is the real thing.
explanation.definitionFit: An ingenue is a naive, unworldly young woman, especially the stock role in a play.

indicators.note: retire means draw back, so the little word to is read backwards

parts.note: hello is a greeting, a salute

explanation.surface: A north African going to bed after a greeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moor' looks like open heathland, but it is Shakespeare's Moor of Venice.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's tragic hero is the Moor of Venice, a North African general.

explanation.surface: A US citizen giving something a pull.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally a person from the United States; as a verb, to pull sharply.

clue.text: Wanderers in transit, perhaps, taking on the orient

indicators.note: taking on means the rearranged letters take in the orient letter
perhaps hints that the letters of the phrase may be arranged otherwise

parts.note: the Orient is the East, abbreviated E

explanation.surface: Travellers on the move heading eastwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges IN TRANSIT into ITINRANTS, and 'taking on' slots E in after ITIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Itinerants are people who travel from place to place, such as nomads or roving workers.
